terms.comment: Literally “unsalted”; more often of a joke or a person: silly.

evidence: Hor. S. 2.4.16: inriguō nihil est ēlūtius hortō
terms.comment: Horace’s word for cabbage from a watered garden, which tastes washed out beside one grown in dry fields.

phrases.latin: Nīl sapit hoc jūs; salem, quaesō.
phrases.english: This soup tastes of nothing; the salt, please.

phrases.latin: cōle suburbānō quī siccīs crēvit in agrīs dulcior: inriguō nihil est ēlūtius hortō
phrases.english: sweeter than a cabbage from the suburbs is one grown in dry fields: nothing is more washed-out than a watered garden’s

phrases.latin: at nunc dīvitibus cēnandī nūlla voluptās, nīl rhombus, nīl damma sapit
phrases.english: but now the rich get no pleasure from dining; turbot tastes of nothing to them, nor venison

sources: Lewis & Short: lenis · Lewis & Short: insulsus · Lewis & Short: eluo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 70, 280.
